audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: The coding (fixed-dominant, rule 01 = stress on the final/main syllable of sesquisyllabic words, not strict) rests on Conver 1999, an SIL phonology sketch in MKS 29; the deciding quotation is verbatim on p.37 of the sealang scan fetched sources during this audit (no file was held before). Two independent descriptions of a different (Lampang, Lower Lamet) variety, Narumol 1980 MA thesis p.27 and its published condensation Narumol 1982 MKS 11 p.37, both fetched sources now, state that the stressed syllable is always the last syllable of the (max. two-syllable) stress group, so three sources across two dialect groups agree. Glottolog lists no reference grammar and web search plus the MKS 44 Palaungic bibliography show no later or instrumental study of Lamet prosody, so Conver 1999 + Narumol 1980/1982 is the best available evidence. sources.citation: Conver 1999, Mon-Khmer Studies 29, pp.36-38 (scanned PDF re-read visually from sealang.net copy)
sources.quote: In a sesquisyllabic word, stress will always fall on the main syllable. That this is a strong characteristic in Lamet is evidenced by the adjustment of loan words to this pattern, given sufficient time.

sources.citation: Conver, Lynn C. 1999. A sketch of the phonology of a Lamet dialect. Mon-Khmer Studies 29:35-56.
sources.quote: 'In a sesquisyllabic word, stress will always fall on the main syllable. That this is a strong characteristic in Lamet is evidenced by the adjustment of loan words to this pattern, given sufficient time. Stress may also be useful as a diagnostic tool to distinguish sesquisyllabic words from compound constructions (i.e., words), which would have stress on both syllables.' p.39: 'because the presyllable is always unstressed, many vowels in this position sound like [schwa-like] in normal paced speech.'

sources.citation: Narumol Charoenma. 1982. The phonologies of a Lampang Lamet and Wiang Papao Lua. Mon-Khmer Studies 11:35-45.
sources.quote: 'The Lamet stress group may have one or two syllables. Each stress group has as its nucleus one strongly stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group. As its periphery it may have an unstressed open syllable or a weakly stressed closed syllable. ... the two permissible patterns are S and sS.'

sources.citation: Narumol Charoenma. 1980. The sound systems of Lampang Lamet and Wiang Papao Lua. M.A. thesis, Mahidol University, Bangkok.
sources.quote: 'The stress group may have one or two syllables. Each stress group has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group, and as its periphery it may have an unstressed syllable or a weakly stressed syllable.' 2.4.3.1: the nuclear (stressed, 'major') syllable 'always occupies the final position'.
